title: Real Estate Investment Funds: How They Work and Why Invest
seoTitle: Real Estate Investment Funds: How They Work and Why Invest
subtitle: Understand the structure, profitability, and opportunities of REITs in Brazil
excerpt: Discover how real estate investment funds operate, their benefits and risks, and how to smartly include them in your portfolio.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
Real Estate Investment Funds (REITs) have gained prominence over recent decades as an accessible alternative for those who wish to participate in the real-estate market without having to purchase a physical property. They combine the return of real-estate assets with the typical liquidity of exchange-traded stocks, offering the Brazilian investor the possibility of receiving monthly income and efficiently diversifying the portfolio.

Context: the rise of REITs in Brazil

Since the enactment of the Real Estate Investment Fund Law in 1993, the sector has experienced steady growth, driven by factors such as declining interest rates, the search for passive income sources, and increased institutional participation in capital markets. Today, REITs represent a significant share of the trading volume on B3, reflecting the confidence of both individual investors and large pension funds.

What Real Estate Investment Funds Are

A REIT is a closed-end condominium that pools resources from various shareholders to acquire, manage, or develop real-estate projects. These projects can be physical properties—such as office buildings, shopping centers, logistics warehouses, or residential units—or financial assets linked to the sector, like Real Estate Receivable Certificates (CRIs) and Real Estate Credit Notes (LCIs).

By purchasing units of a REIT, the investor becomes an indirect owner of a fraction of the assets that compose the fund. This ownership confers the right to receive income generated by rents or credit operations associated with the portfolio, which are distributed periodically, usually on a monthly basis.

How REITs Work in Practice

The operation of a REIT can be divided into three main stages:

  1. Capital raising: The fund manager launches units in the primary market, typically through a public offering. Investors subscribe to these units, sending capital to the fund.
  2. Investment and management: The manager uses the resources to purchase properties or credit rights, aiming to generate cash flow. Management includes property maintenance, lease contract negotiations, and monitoring occupancy and profitability indicators.
  3. Income distribution: Received rents (or interest from credit securities) are passed on to unit holders after deducting operating expenses and the management fee. The distribution policy usually requires at least 95% of net profit to be paid out, ensuring regular earnings.

REITs are traded on the stock exchange like any other share, providing daily liquidity to the investor. If a shareholder wishes to sell their units, they simply place an order on B3, and the transaction settles within a few business days. This feature eliminates the need to wait for a direct buyer, as is common in the traditional real-estate market.

Regarding taxation, income distributed by REITs is exempt from Income Tax for individuals, provided the fund meets certain requirements—such as having at least 50 unit holders and not being controlled by a legal entity. Capital gains realized on the sale of units, on the other hand, are subject to the standard 15% rate.

Practical Implications for the Brazilian Investor

For those intending to include REITs in their investment strategy, several points are essential:

  • Risk profile: Although REITs offer regular earnings, they are not risk-free. Vacancy, tenant default, and fluctuations in property values can affect distributions.
  • Sector diversification: There are REITs focused on different segments—offices, retail, logistics, residential, hospitals—allowing investors to adjust exposure according to the economic outlook of each sector.
  • Liquidity and investment horizon: The ability to trade on the exchange enables short-term portfolio adjustments, but volatility may increase during economic crises.
  • Costs: In addition to the management fee (typically between 0.5% and 2% per year), there may be performance fees and brokerage costs when buying or selling units.
  • Tax aspects: Investors must stay aware of capital-gain tax and the reporting of income in the annual Income Tax return.

A recommended practice is to start exposure with well-established funds that have a history of high occupancy and transparent management. Analyzing monthly reports, checking tenant quality, and evaluating the average contract term are indicators that help gauge cash-flow stability.

Conclusion

Real Estate Investment Funds consolidate themselves as an instrument that merges the attractiveness of tangible assets with the dynamism of capital markets. By offering periodic earnings, daily liquidity, and the possibility of sector diversification, they present a viable alternative both for investors seeking passive income and for those who wish to complement an equity or fixed-income portfolio. However, like any investment, success depends on understanding the risks, carefully selecting funds, and continuously monitoring performance indicators. When used wisely, REITs can play a strategic role in building long-term wealth in the Brazilian economic scenario.
